text: From Hemlock Pass the route follows the ridgeline toward Bryant Peak, angling right behind trees to a brushy notch, then climbs roughly 170 ft to a meadow at the base of a talus slope that covers about three-quarters of the peak's base. The final scramble goes up rock on the left (or, when snow-free, around the exposed north side) to the summit; the rock is loose and helmets are recommended.

edits.old: to a meadow at the base of a talus slope that covers about three-quarters of the peak's base
edits.new: to a meadow below a talus slope that blankets roughly three-quarters of the peak's foot

text: Traverse the south side of the west shoulder to the summit block, then scramble the loose rock on the left, or when snow-free go around the exposed north side. The first high point may be a false summit, with a short exposed traverse to the true top at 5,801 ft. Helmets are recommended.

text: From I-90 Exit 47, take Denny Creek Road (FR 58) about 3 miles, past Denny Creek Campground, then turn left onto FR 5830 to the Denny Creek trailhead (~2,300 ft). Follow the Denny Creek Trail (#1014, the Melakwa Lake trail) up the valley past waterfalls, then up steeper switchbacks to Hemlock Pass, about 4 miles and roughly 2,300 ft above the car. At the crest of the pass turn right and follow the ridge on a bearing of about 33°, skirting cliff bands mainly on the left, to a plateau and meadow on the ridge. Early in the season, while snow still covers the brush, a brushy notch behind trees on the right leads about 170 ft up and then northeast to a meadow at the foot of the talus field that wraps about three-quarters of the peak's base; later in the season that line is choked with brush, so stay on the ridge and go straight up it to the summit block. The final scramble is loose rock on the left, or when snow-free around the exposed north side; helmets are recommended. The round trip is about 9 miles with roughly 3,600 ft of gain for Bryant alone; adding nearby Hemlock Peak makes it about 9.5 miles and 3,900 ft.

edits.new: a brushy notch behind trees on the right climbs about 170 ft, then heads northeast, arriving at a meadow beside the foot of the talus field

text:
Start at Trinity at the end of the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, at about 2,800 ft. Take the Buck Creek trail #1513, which splits off the Chiwawa River trail within the first mile and climbs steadily to Buck Creek Pass — roughly six hours and about 3,100 ft of gain.

Why this way round at all is worth understanding before you commit: Buck sits only about three miles from Trinity as the crow flies and is Class 2-3 from the south-west, but a long rugged ridge runs north and south of it and there is no road or trail up the Napeequa on the west, so the normal route is a very long way round. The two documented ways to reach that west side are the high route north from Buck Creek Pass and Little Giant Pass from the south.

At the pass there is a large established camp with toilets just before the switchbacks up toward Liberty Cap. Fill up with water there — there is none for the next four miles and the ridge walk is fully sun-exposed.

Follow the old High Pass trail as it winds high around the side of Liberty Cap, then south for several miles until the tread dies out in talus and hard snowfields at High Pass; crampons are worth having for that. Contour through the pass and under Mount Berge, then angle up to the ridge crest just south of Point 7839. A short section of Class 3 reaches a faint saddle from which there is an easy walk-off down into Louis Creek Basin.

edits.new: the next four miles have none, and the ridge walk

edits.new: as it curves high along the flank of Liberty Cap

text: From the Upper Big Quilcene Trailhead, Trail #833 climbs through old-growth forest past Shelter Rock Camp and Camp Mystery to the open alpine gap of Marmot Pass (~6,000 ft), one of the most scenic passes in the Olympics. From the pass, turn right onto the Tubal Cain Trail and follow it north about 100 m to a junction, then leave it and climb right up switchbacks along the ridge, over a minor ~6,800 ft knob, to Buckhorn's southwest summit (6,988 ft) — the higher of its two nearly-equal summits. The final approach is loose scree, not quite Class 3, finishing with a short scramble onto a large summit boulder. When snow-free, the route requires no technical gear or roped travel.

text: From Quilcene, drive US 101 south about 1.5 miles and turn right (west) onto Penny Creek Road. After about 1.5 miles bear left onto Big Quilcene River Road, FR 27, and follow it about 9.25 miles to FR 2750. Turn left and drive about 4.75 miles on this narrow, single-lane road to the Upper Big Quilcene Trailhead at its end, about 2,600 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park; no wilderness permit is required for a day trip.

text: The North Face is 1,300 feet of 40-50 degree snow and ice climbed in approximately 8-13 pitches, most belayed. Work left of any bergschrund, back right to center of lower face and straight up. Upper rock cliffs force several pitches leftward in a rising traverse. Within 200 feet of summit go left around a craggy-looking outcrop at the end of upper cliffs, then back rightward to gain the summit. The face is wind-scoured in places requiring careful assessment of stability. Route quality varies significantly by conditions; some ascents report ice-hard wind-scoured snow while others encounter moderate powder.

edits.old: Work left of any bergschrund, back right to center of lower face and straight up. Upper rock cliffs force several pitches leftward in a rising traverse. Within 200 feet of summit go left around a craggy-looking outcrop at the end of upper cliffs, then back rightward to gain the summit.
edits.new: Stay left of any bergschrund, then cut back right to the middle of the lower face and head directly upward. Cliffs of rock higher on the face push the route leftward over several pitches as a rising traverse. When you are within 200 feet of the top, pass a craggy-looking outcrop on its left, where the upper cliffs end, then swing back to the right to reach the summit.

text: Start from the Boston Basin Trailhead (~3,200 ft), about 21.7 miles up Cascade River Road from Marblemount (a separate, shorter-drive trailhead than the Cascade Pass TH used for the SW route). The unmaintained climbers' path follows an old, overgrown mining road for about 1 mile to a former mine site, then becomes a steep boot-path through old-growth forest with roughly four creek/stream crossings, emerging above treeline around 5,300 ft into Boston Basin — about 2.5 miles and 3,100 ft of gain, typically 3-4 hours. Boston Basin has two designated backcountry camps used as base for this route: low camp (~5,300 ft) and high camp (~6,300-6,400 ft); an NPS permit is required and camping is restricted to these established sites. From high camp, follow the Quien Sabe Glacier route, roping up for crevasses, and climb toward Sharkfin Col (rather than the loose class 3-4 scramble around Boston Peak). Many parties gain the ridge just east of Sharkfin Col, where a natural/fixed sling anchor is commonly used to make a short rappel — or, in leaner conditions, a steep no-fall-zone downclimb on crumbly mixed rock — down onto the Boston Glacier; multiple trip reports flag this as the technical crux of the approach, sometimes harder than the climbing above. Once on the Boston Glacier (one of the largest glaciers in the lower 48), rope up and traverse south toward the base of Buckner's north face, zig-zagging around a bergschrund and large crevasses near the toe of the face, with some rock scrambling to bypass the 'schrund. Many parties bivy on the glacier itself (~7,800 ft) to shorten summit day. From the base, the North Face climbs about 1,300 ft of 40-50 degree snow/ice: work left of the bergschrund, then back right to the center of the lower face and straight up until upper rock cliffs force a rising traverse leftward; within about 200 ft of the summit, go left around a craggy rock outcrop, then back right to the top. Competent parties in good nick conditions often solo this face; less experienced or larger parties belay it with pickets/ice screws. Glacier travel, the Sharkfin Col rappel/downclimb, and typical alpine hazards (rockfall, afternoon softening, weather) are the main approach concerns.

edits.old: work left of the bergschrund, then back right to the center of the lower face and straight up until upper rock cliffs force a rising traverse leftward
edits.new: keep left of the bergschrund, then cut back right to the middle of the lower face and head directly up until the rock cliffs above push you into a rising traverse to the left

text: The standard descent does not reverse the North Face — parties continue over the summit and go down Buckner's southwest slopes. From the top, descend gullies, scree, and snow on the fall line to about 7,200 ft, then traverse down and right across Horseshoe Basin on a broad ledge system at 6,200-6,400 ft (passing near the old Davenport Mine) to a snow finger; ascend the snow finger about 100 ft to regain the rounded ridge above the toe of Sahale's south ridge. Scramble roughly 40 ft up short rock steps, then follow paths through heather and rock for about 300 ft along the ridge crest (with the Davenport Glacier in view), before traversing up and left on slabs and snow above the glacier debris to the moraine flats beneath Sahale. From here, parties who arranged a car shuttle can continue over Sahale Arm and out Cascade Pass; most parties who started at Boston Basin instead re-climb Sahale's south ridge back toward Sharkfin Col and reverse the Quien Sabe Glacier approach to Boston Basin and the trailhead — some elect to 'carry over' with full packs and skip returning to a Boston Basin camp entirely. The southwest-slopes portion of the descent itself is a scree/snow walk-off with no rappelling (0 rappels). However, on the return leg back through Sharkfin Col, expect the same technical step encountered on approach: many parties make one short rappel (a single rope length off the natural/fixed sling anchor at the col is sufficient — no multi-pitch rappelling reported) to get back down onto or off the glacier side, while others downclimb it unroped depending on conditions and party comfort; in bad weather/whiteout, at least one party describes rappelling a steep ice gully near a nearby col with pickets as an alternate exit. Treat this Sharkfin Col step, not the summit slopes, as the route's real technical/rappel hazard.

edits.old: traversing up and left on slabs and snow above the glacier debris
edits.new: traversing leftward and upward across slabs and snow over the glacier debris

text: Buckner Mountain is the third-highest peak in North Cascades National Park, the 14th-highest summit in Washington, and 11th on the state's Bulger list of 100 highest peaks — one of only about ten non-volcanic Washington summits above 9,000 ft. The mountain has two summits of nearly equal height a short distance apart along the summit ridge; nearly all parties top out on the southwest (true) summit reached by this route. It crowns the ridge between Sahale Arm and Horseshoe Basin and is a coveted objective on multi-day Cascade Pass carryovers with Sahale and Boston Peak. The southwest side gives the standard non-technical line — long, but largely third- and fourth-class scrambling — most commonly reached from a high camp on Sahale Arm.

edits.old: Buckner Mountain is the third-highest peak in North Cascades National Park, the 14th-highest summit in Washington
edits.new: Buckner Mountain ranks third among the peaks of North Cascades National Park and is the 14th-highest summit in Washington

text: From Bullseye Pass (~6,200 ft), parties drop packs and climb the steep southeast slope on foot/hands to grippy granite, working up and over a hump before dropping beneath the summit on its western side (Class 3 traverse). The final approach to the true summit follows the south ridge and requires roped Class 4-5.0 climbing — two independent accounts describe one to two short pitches on excellent, hold-covered granite, finishing with an exposed high step onto a one-person summit perch.

text: Huge pale talus in a northwest-facing couloir, then two points at a notch — the right-hand one is the top. From the basin, hike around Upper Chain Lake and climb the couloir above it. Low down the slope is a deceptively complex mix of steep heather, mossy slabs, bushes and short cliffs; the clean, huge, whitish talus higher up is what tells you that you are into the correct couloir rather than picking your way up the general hillside. It tops out at a notch between two points on the crest, and from that notch it is genuinely not obvious which is higher — take the right-hand, southern one. That is the summit, and the last stretch to it turns looser and sandier. The negative marker is a different summit sharing this name: a lower, fang-shaped tower southeast of the trail pass between the Chain and Doelle basins, shaped like a giant cuspid, which takes Class 4 and 5 climbing and rappels to get off. If you are standing under a spire that plainly needs a rope, you are beneath that one. The high point described here is bulky, and nothing about it is tooth-like.

text: Burnt Boot Peak (P 6480) sits across the Middle Fork of the Snoqualmie River, about two miles southeast of Big Snow Mountain. From the base of the steepest part of the north ridge, three leads of fifth class on granite, the last along a very sharp crest, reach easier ground; three more leads of class 3 and 4 gain the summit. The peak's first ascent, by a 1963 survey party, came by an easier scramble line. No repeat ascents of the ridge are recorded, so expect little to no modern traffic.

edits.new: Starting at the foot of the steepest section of the north ridge, three leads

text: From the Eightmile Trail, cut cross-country up through an old burn zone, then continue up and left toward the gully between the S and SE ridges. The S/SE gully is wide and offers a 'choose your own adventure' character: the center/right line is mostly class 2, while the climbers-left side holds solid class 3-4 rock. The gully tops out at roughly 8,150 ft, about 360 vertical feet below the 8,501 ft top. This line cuts the standard 8-9 mile one-way West Ridge approach roughly in half.

text: This route starts with a boat crossing of Ross Lake (Ross Lake Resort water taxi, or a private/inflatable boat carried in via the 0.6-mile portage trail from the SR-20 pullout), landing at the Lightning Creek Trailhead near the head of the lake at roughly 1,500 ft. From the shoreline, follow the Lightning Creek Trail north; parties with their own boat commonly start pre-dawn (around 4am) to leave enough daylight for the long day above, while the water taxi runs only from 8am to 5pm. After about 2 hours of hiking, watch for the junction with the old, no-longer-maintained Freezeout Creek Trail. The first stretch above the junction is the trickiest routefinding on the whole approach: steep rock-and-alder slopes that require a rising, diagonal ascent line before you regain proper forest and trail tread — recent parties note intermittent orange flagging tape marking this stretch, which is worth watching for. Once back in the trees, tread on the Freezeout Creek Trail improves to 'decent shape' as you climb to the Freezeout Cabin at about 3,600 ft, sited immediately after a creek crossing; the cabin (maintained bunks, wood stove, logbook) is a good psychological waypoint and emergency shelter. About a quarter mile past the cabin, cross Freezeout Creek again and pass through an old burn. Trail tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft, but the bushwhacking through here is described as minimal. From there, stay on the west side of Freezeout Creek, hiking roughly 50-100 ft above the waterline, which gives the most open going through 5,000 ft. At 5,000 ft, cross to the south/east side of the drainage, where the terrain opens into meadow and talus. Above this, climb steep red heather, talus, and scree to a notch on the peak's southwest ridge at about 7,600 ft. From the notch, the final roughly 700-750 vertical feet to the 8,300+ ft summit is class 2 with short class 3 sections. Total one-way distance from the lakeshore to the summit is on the order of 16-17 miles with close to 7,000 ft of gain from the boat landing alone (the 8,500 ft gain figure reflects the day's cumulative up-and-down, not just net elevation). Freezeout Creek is the reliable water source for essentially the entire approach up to about 5,000-5,500 ft; carry water above that, since there is no dependable source on the upper heather/talus/scree slopes or the summit ridge. Because of the remoteness and boat-access logistics, this is realistically a long single push (18+ hours car-to-car including the taxi) or a one-night backpack, not a casual day hike.

edits.old: climb steep red heather, talus, and scree to a notch on the peak's southwest ridge at about 7,600 ft
edits.new: work up steep red heather, then talus and scree, to a notch at about 7,600 ft on the peak's southwest ridge

text: Despite the north face already hosting several routes since its 1979 first ascent, the central buttress directly below the summit remained untouched until Morgan Zentler and Jason Schilling's 2017 ascent. They started with easy 5th-class climbing to escape the rockfall line, then hit a crux pitch (pitch 2) of mid-5.10/5.11-ish face climbing requiring a short aid move. Subsequent pitches traverse out of a dihedral on a tricky flake and surmount a roof on the left via fun but hard cracks and stemming; the middle section demanded extensive cleaning of dirt- and moss-covered slabs. After about five pitches the route gains the ridge proper, where the rock quality improves and climbing becomes more moderate, aside from one short, harder hand-and-fist crack. The final technical pitch dances delicately around teetering blocks before moderate snow slopes lead the last 400 ft to the summit.

edits.old: aside from one short, harder hand-and-fist crack
edits.new: apart from a single short but harder hand-and-fist crack

text: The lawful approach is from the US side: cross Ross Lake by boat, follow the Lightning Creek trail and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail, then work round to the glacier below the north face. The first-ascent party instead came in from Canada — from Lightning Lake in Manning Provincial Park, BC, up and over Frosty Mountain, into Princess Creek basin, across the Princess/Crow Creek divide and down into the Crow Creek drainage — but walking into the US away from a port of entry is not a lawful crossing. On that line the first-ascent party camped on the only dry spot on the ridge, about two-thirds of the way down to the approach glacier.

edits.old: camped on the only dry spot on the ridge, about two-thirds of the way down to the approach glacier
edits.new: made camp at the one dry spot along the ridge, about two-thirds of the descent to the approach glacier

text:
The north face is a wall of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs about fourteen hundred feet high, holding ice or the remnants of it, with a glacier at its foot. It carries several routes and they are not marked, so identification is by position against the summit and nothing else.

The test is simple and it is the whole identification: this route takes the central buttress, and that buttress sits directly below the summit. Stand back on the glacier, find the summit on the skyline, and drop a plumb line from it. The buttress under that line is this route. If the summit is off to one side from where you are standing, you are under a different climb.

Getting onto it is the second problem. Expect an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock, and start with easy fifth-class ground whose purpose is to get out of the rockfall line rather than to climb anything — that first pitch is a position move, not a feature.

Confirm on pitch two, because it arrives fast and it is unmistakable: the crux comes almost immediately, mid-fifth-class face climbing hard enough that the first ascent used a short aid move to pass it. A wall this size whose hardest pitch is the second one is unusual, and it is the strongest evidence you are on line.

The middle of the route then traverses out of a dihedral on a tricky flake and takes a roof on the left via cracks and stemming, over slabs that needed heavy cleaning of dirt and moss. After about five pitches the route gains the ridge proper and the rock quality improves markedly, with one short harder hand-and-fist crack. The final technical pitch picks its way around teetering blocks, and then moderate snow slopes run the last four hundred feet to the top.

Negative marker: if your line starts in a blocky set of face holds beside a gully or chimney at the left edge of the buttress, you are on the neighbouring route at the buttress's left margin, and higher up it follows a distinctive yellow quartz dyke that this route does not touch.

Descent is not the climb reversed. Walk off the south side and the east ridge back toward camp.

edits.old: with one short harder hand-and-fist crack
edits.new: plus a single short, harder hand-and-fist crack

text:
Read the legal point first. This line walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and then crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it requires prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is the first-ascent line, not a recommendation.

It starts from the lake in the provincial park, climbs up and over Frosty Mountain, descends into the next creek basin to the south, traverses to the divide, and drops into the Crow Creek drainage below the peak's north face. The first ascent camped on the only dry spot on the ridge, roughly two-thirds of the way down toward the glacier.

The wholly lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west.

text: There is no climbers' trail to the base. A party who got there reported finding none and navigating purely off photographs, so stop looking for tread and navigate by the landform. The landform is the deep gully that separates Cathedral Peak from The Monk, the semi-detached tower on the lower right side of the south face. One published account leaves the maintained trail at the first switchback after Cathedral Pass and heads for the gully from there; others come across the parkland between Upper Cathedral Lake and the pass. Both end up in the same place, thirty to sixty minutes from camp. Go up into the gully — do not stop at its mouth. Three accounts put the start of the first pitch about 150 feet up the Cathedral–Monk gully, on the left wall, which is the Cathedral side. Scramble onto a tall pedestal there; it gives a decent belay stance to start from. Pedestal, left wall, about 150 feet in: that is the whole identification. How to tell this from the South Face routes, and it is a simple physical test: is there a semi-detached tower standing between you and the wall? If yes, you are at the SE Buttress, which follows the ridge behind The Monk on the right-hand edge of the south face. If you are walking up to an open face with nothing in front of it, that is the South Face route, a different and much harder climb. A related trap in the naming rather than on the ground: The Monk has its own south face with its own routes on it. Beta headed South Face may be describing the tower, not the mountain. Coming down, the descent is the walk-off to the west and then south-west back toward Upper Cathedral Lake, and its crux is a gap the route description tells you to hop across. It can be avoided by downclimbing the exposed nose beside it and stepping over — easy when dry, but no-fall ground.

text:
From I-90 exit 80 at Cle Elum, take SR-903 north through Roslyn and Ronald along Cle Elum Lake for about 14.8 miles, then gravel Cle Elum Valley Road / FR 4330 for 12.3 miles and the short NF-153 spur to the Cathedral Rock trailhead, Trail #1345, at about 3,350 ft. Sign the free self-issue wilderness permit.

The trail climbs through old growth to Nosh Nosh Wahtum, formerly Squaw Lake, at about 4,850 ft and 2.5 miles, then opens into meadow with Cathedral Rock ahead. At about 4 miles you reach Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft and the PCT junction.

Walk north on the PCT for a couple of minutes, then cut across the meadow to a stand of trees. Parties cache the gear they do not need on the climb there. From the trees, start a rising traverse under the east face, past the meadows, and then across a loose talus slope with the northeast buttress in sight.

About 6.4 km and 3,400 ft.

text:
The route starts at the top of a short, steep snowfield, and that snowfield is the arrival test. Crossing the loose talus under the east face you come to it; it is short but steep enough that parties in approach shoes have picked their way up it holding stones for security. Reaching the top of that snow patch is reaching the start of the climbing.

And here is the mistake parties actually make at that point, which is the most useful thing to know about this route: at the top of the snow it is natural to exit right onto ledges and start up from there. That is wrong. A party that does it finds the ground harder than the fourth class the description promises, wanders left, right and up, and comes back down. The correct start is to exit back left into the moat at the top of the snow, where the terrain is much easier.

So the test is a difficulty test: if your first moves off the snow feel harder than fourth class, you are on the wrong side of the snowfield. Go back and take the moat on the left.

What should follow: easy ground you can simul-climb, then a ledge system that traverses rightward toward the crest of the buttress. The buttress runs about seven pitches and 900 ft, 5.7, grade III. A route that is sustained from the first pitch is not it.

And one thing to settle before you leave the trees: this peak is descended by the south side, not by reversing the buttress. Note where you came up.

text: From Cathedral Pass (or via the Peggy's Pond Trail), scramble up the south ridge/rounded spur to about 6,400 ft where it meets the summit formation. Climb the obvious gully on its upper-left side, left of the South Buttress, then continue up the southwest face to the ridge crest. Most parties choose to rope up for one short, awkward-angle 5th-class pitch off the ridge crest; from there it's a class-4 scramble to the true summit. Rockfall in the gully is the defining hazard of the route, especially once it melts out of snow later in the season.

text:
Drive the Cle Elum River Road, SR 903, to Salmon La Sac, then keep right just past the ranger station onto the rough Forest Road 4330 and follow it about twelve miles to the road end at roughly 3,350 ft.

There are two trailheads within a few yards of each other at the road end and this is the first place to go wrong. The Hyas Lake and Deception Pass trail heads north. You want the Cathedral Rock trail, #1345, heading west, and it may be signed slightly before the road actually ends. Vehicle break-ins have been a recurring problem at this trailhead, which is a pattern rather than a one-off.

The trail reaches Squaw Lake at about two and a half miles and continues to Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft, roughly four miles in with about 3,400 ft of gain. Turn left, west, onto the Pacific Crest Trail. In less than half a mile you reach the junction with Trail #1375 to Peggy's Pond.

At that junction two climbers' paths head toward the peak, and the counter-intuitive one is the right choice: the left path looks from a distance like the wrong way, but it avoids a scree slope and gives some scrambling instead. Either goes, but do not talk yourself out of the left one on appearances.

text: From the summit, most parties reverse toward the notch/col below the summit block and descend the gully on the south side of the east face (sometimes described as the same gully used by the Northeast Buttress descent). Expect a mix of downclimbing and rappelling: parties commonly do two double-rope (60m) rappels — the first from trees/rock anchors near the head of the gully with some downclimbing to reach the next station, and a second double-rope rappel that reaches easier snow near the gully's base — though some parties describe reaching the base with a single 60m rappel plus downclimbing depending on snow coverage. Anchors are a mix of natural gear (trees, rock horns/slings) rather than bolts; bring cord/webbing to back up or replace tattered slings. From the base of the gully, downclimb snow/talus east back into the Chair Peak basin and pick up the approach trail to Source Lake and out. Watch for cornices at the gully lip early season, loose rock in the gully when snow-free, and wet-slide hazard on the descent slopes during warm spring conditions.

text: The two counts on this page are the same descent with a different rope setup, not a disagreement. The gully on the south side of the east face goes in one 60 m double-rope rappel, or in the two ~30 m single-rope rappels listed here. How much you rappel at all depends on conditions: with good steep snow much of it is downclimbed, and parties describe reaching the base on a single rappel plus downclimbing. Two rappel stations were added in early summer 2023 so that a 60 m rope makes every rappel on the route - several leave under 5 ft of rope spare, so knot the ends.

text: From the upper Alpental parking lot (I-90 Exit 52, end of Alpental Road), follow the Alpental Valley/Source Lake trail: the first 0.5 mile follows the old ski-area cat track, then it becomes a standard trail climbing gently through forest for about 0.75 mile to Source Lake (roughly 1.25-1.75 miles and a few hundred feet of gain from the car). From Source Lake, leave the maintained trail and head cross-country/up boot path toward the basin below Chair Peak's east face (~4200 ft), a further 0.5-1 mile with steeper talus, heather, and (early/mid season) snow slopes. From the basin, climb a short snow gully for approximately 300 ft to gain the crest of the ridge that forms the Northeast Buttress, then follow the ridge to the start of the technical climbing. Total approach is on the order of 2-2.5 miles and 1,700-2,000 ft of gain one-way to the base of the buttress. Hazards: the basin and approach gully sit below avalanche terrain off Chair Peak and Snoqualmie Mountain — this is a classic early-season slide path, and parties often describe deep postholing, wet-slab activity, and wind-loaded slopes here; a rope/axe/crampons are typically carried from the basin onward given the exposure of the approach gully itself.

text:
Thumbtack Rock is the decision point, and the turn is right and up a grassy gully. Everything else on this side of the mountain continues straight on up the basin to the foot of the east face. This route is the one that leaves at the Thumbtack and crosses the divide. A published fix for the Thumbtack is 10T 0616013E 5257415N. If you are still walking up the basin under a big east face, you have gone past the turn.

The start itself is a saddle with trees on it, and the first pitch goes up the gully to the left of that saddle. Trees on a saddle, gully immediately left — that pairing is the arrival test, and both halves are visible from below in poor light.

Confirmation one pitch up, which is the strongest signal on the route: pitch one runs about 200 ft to the crest and you belay off trees on the south side of the ridge. From those trees you scramble down and left to a chimney-shaped feature with a chockstone jammed at its top. You cannot see that chockstone from the trees; it becomes obvious as soon as you scramble across. A chockstone-capped chimney at the end of a short downward scramble means you are on the northwest ridge and nothing else.

Negative tests: if your first pitch is bolted, you are on Voie de Chaise on the east face. If you are looking up at a big buttress from the head of the basin, you never made the Thumbtack turn.

text: From the Alpental lot at about 3,100 ft, take the summer trail toward Source Lake. Where the trail meets the talus field, do NOT drop down — dropping is the turn for The Tooth. Instead hold your height and gain 100 to 200 horizontal feet until you can pass small cliff bands on your right. Above them the tread improves and runs just below a waterfall. Leave the trail at a longer talus field, usually marked by a large cairn, and climb up and left on good paths between the talus to the permanent snow patch under the east face. Climb the snow patch to its top, then take the last 200 to 300 ft of loose scree, keeping hard against the base of the peak where the scree lies at a gentler angle. Reckon two to three hours from the car to the foot of the route.

text:
The line of bolts is the test, and it is the only one you need in cloud. This is a fully bolted alpine sport line. Every other route that starts on this side of Chair Peak is climbed on gear. If you cannot see a bolt from the ground, you are not at the start of this route, whatever the terrain looks like.

Where along the base: at the top of the scree there is a band of third and fourth class rock that guards the right-hand side of Chair Peak. The route starts just past the left edge of that band. So walk the base leftward until the guarding band ends, and the first bolted line past it is this one.

What pitch one feels like, as confirmation: a few tricky moves straight off the ground at about 5.7, and then it eases into sustained, clean 5.6 slab for roughly 120 ft. Hard slab on clean rock with bolts is right. Broken blocky ground, or a chimney, is not.

How to tell it from the East Face route, which is the mistake worth avoiding: the first-ascent party deliberately kept this line clear of the East Face, and the East Face both starts and finishes well to the right of it. So if you are at a gear start on broken rock, you have not walked far enough left along the base.

And the descent gives you a back-bearing: the ordinary Chair Peak gully descent lands you only about a hundred feet uphill of this route's base. A party coming down that gully that walks a hundred feet downhill is standing at the start.

text:
From the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166, the boot path drops to Early Winters Creek, crosses on logs, and climbs the timbered rib to the bench camp at 6,400-6,600 ft and on up the loose main gully to Burgundy Col.

This is the 1952 first ascent of Chianti Spire itself.
